platforms.title: A Song Predicted the Dice Game at the Cross
platforms.description:
Ten centuries before the cross, a song recorded exactly how a dying man's clothes would be divided up.

Psalm 22. David wrote it in the first person, but David was never executed; he died an old man. He was describing someone else: stripped, surrounded, his life poured out. And one line lands with strange precision: "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture" (Psalm 22:18, KJV).

A thousand years later, John stood at the cross and watched soldiers divide Jesus' clothes, then cast lots for the seamless coat, "that the scripture might be fulfilled."

God had it written down early so that when it happened, you would know: the cross was no accident. It was the plan. They rolled dice for the clothes off his back, never seeing what he was doing: laying down his life to win you back.

platforms.label: YouTube (Long-form 16:9)
platforms.title: Psalm 22 Recorded the Cross a Thousand Years Early
platforms.description:
A thousand years before Rome invented crucifixion as public theatre outside Jerusalem, King David wrote a song in the first person about a man stripped, surrounded, and poured out to death. But David himself was never executed. He died an old man, in his bed.

So who is the song about?

Watch one line: "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture" (Psalm 22:18, KJV). The dying man's killers divide his clothes between them, then gamble for one piece.

At the cross, the apostle John watched Roman soldiers do exactly that: divide Jesus' garments into parts, then cast lots for the seamless coat rather than tear it, "that the scripture might be fulfilled" (John 19:24). The soldiers were not reading Psalms. They were gambling. And every throw of the dice landed on a line written ten centuries early.

In this piece: why David's psalm cannot be about David, the strange precision of verse eighteen, John's eyewitness citation, and what it means that God published the plan of the cross a millennium in advance.

The suffering man of Psalm 22 has a name: Jesus. They rolled dice for the clothes off his back, never seeing what he was really doing: laying down his life to win you back.

redteam:
VERDICT: PASS

- Verbatim: the only quoted verse span, "They part my garments among them, and cast
  lots upon my vesture", is the exact KJV given, character for character, in every
  platform that quotes it. "that the scripture might be fulfilled" is quoted as John's
  phrase and matches John 19:24 KJV. Clean.
- Typography: all-ASCII, no em-dashes, no smart quotes. Clean.
- Titles: "A Song Predicted the Dice Game at the Cross" is a true curiosity hook (the
  lots ARE a dice-like gamble; the psalm DOES predate it by ~10 centuries). "David
  Wrote His Own Execution - But He Died in Bed" is honest and the video's own argument.
  No sensationalism, no overclaim.
- Thread match: garments/lots/John's citation is exactly the piece's spine. The copy
  never promises more than the video shows.
- Platform fit: TikTok/IG hook in the first line and short; FB carries the verse;
  the long description sets up the deep-dive structure honestly.
- Nothing blocking. Ship it.
